About

M1 student at Télécom Paris on the applied algebra track (advanced math courses in info theory, cryptography, coding theory, and quantum info) and MODS track (economics, management, law and ethics, sociology, digital transformation, and innovation). I learn through building; refer to my projects to discover my passion for building.

I also teach. I founded Quantum In Africa, which has reached 800+ students across three countries, and I was a teaching assistant for algorithms at AddisCoder in Addis Ababa, a summer camp for Ethiopian high schoolers led by Prof. Jelani Nelson.

I joined Télécom Paris in 2025 after two years of preparatory classes (MPSI/PSI*) at IPEST. I am looking for internships in machine learning and quantum technology.

Writings

Essays on teaching, quantum computing and what I am building.

Oct 2026 · 4 min read Reflection on Teaching Computer Science in Ethiopia Four weeks as a teaching assistant at AddisCoder in Addis Ababa, and what 150 Ethiopian high schoolers taught me.

I spent four weeks in Addis Ababa as a teaching assistant at AddisCoder, a summer program where about 150 Ethiopian high schoolers learn programming and algorithms. I arrived expecting to teach. I left having learned just as much.

A different clock

On my first morning I had breakfast with two Ethiopians, an American and a Swede. Someone asked the time and I said it was 9 a.m. Eyob corrected me: “No, it’s 3 o’clock!” Ethiopians count the hours from sunrise, which makes sense close to the equator, where the length of the day barely changes through the year.

The calendar is different too. It runs about seven years behind the Gregorian one, so a colleague’s ID card saying he was born in 1996 meant 2003 in the calendar I use.

Music, food and faith

Every Friday I went with other teachers to the Fendika cultural centre for jazz, traditional music and performances. Those evenings were my way into a culture I barely knew, and a relaxed place to talk with my colleagues.

Coming from Tunisia, I am used to spicy food, yet some Ethiopian spices were too much even for me. I loved injera, the flatbread made from fermented teff flour that comes with almost every meal. Addis also surprised me with its range of restaurants: Indian, Chinese, Korean, Iraqi and European.

I also attended a Debre celebration, where branches are gathered and burned as a huge torch called a chibo while groups of young people sing “Hoya Hoye”. Many Ethiopians fast several times a year, sometimes for more than forty days, and eat no animal products during that time.

By the end of the program I even knew a little Amharic. Add “-ye” to a noun and it becomes “my”, so my sister Lyna became “Lynaye”.

In the classroom

The students came from all over the country and were split into six labs by language and programming level. Ethiopia has more than 80 languages, and although most students spoke English, some struggled to express themselves in it. That taught me that a difficulty in class is not always about knowledge. A student can understand an idea, or solve a problem, and still be unable to phrase the question in English.

In my lab, Yahya and Darneim spoke Arabic. My Tunisian dialect is different from theirs, but we managed, and I could explain programming ideas in Arabic and switch to English a few minutes later. I learned to reformulate an idea several times, give a concrete example, or cut the reasoning into smaller steps. The goal was never to hand over the answer, but to find an explanation that let the student keep going alone. Ethiopian teachers also came into the labs to redo exercises at the board in the group’s main local language, so students could focus on the content instead of the language.

What the students taught me

Some students arrived having barely touched a computer and left having studied graph algorithms. Admission is selective, with about 150 chosen from several thousand applicants, but what struck me was their persistence. They kept working on hard exercises and fixed their own mistakes.

I had lunch with them every day. We talked about cartoons, European football and food, ate injera almost daily, and tried to debug Python together. Those lunches built trust, and trust made the lab work easier.

They also told me what some of them had been through: periods without enough food, conflict in their region, three years of interrupted schooling, and school computer rooms with few machines. Having a computer, a connection and a place to work feels normal in some places, but it is not a given everywhere. Still, they were optimistic. Many dream of top universities, encouraged by AddisCoder alumni who went on to Yale and Princeton. It reminded me not to reduce a person to the obstacles they face.

I had already noticed differences in transport, housing and public services when I moved from Tunisia to France the year before. Ethiopia widened that perspective: hardship and privilege are relative to where you live. I came home grateful, and wanting to help make education reach people who have less access to it. I do not think there is a simple fix for these inequalities, but I believe even small educational efforts can open up opportunities.

On the last day the students threw us a party, with a cake, thank-you speeches and gifts, including framed artworks. The gifts were lovely, but what touched me most was how sincere the gesture was.

The team

I was shy at first, but the other teachers were very sociable and we quickly became a real group, with hikes, bowling and card game nights. We came from Spain, Sweden, China, the United States, South Korea, Ethiopia, India and Brazil. Working with such different backgrounds taught me to listen to other ways of thinking.

Every Friday we graded about 150 exams. Working as a chain, each teacher took one question while others entered the scores and computed the final grades, and we finished in about two hours. Splitting the work only pays off with a shared method: everyone has to know what is expected.

What I take away

AddisCoder gave me much more than teaching experience. I improved my teaching, my English and my ability to communicate across cultures. Most of all, I learned to understand the people around me, to adapt to new situations, and to appreciate the opportunities I have. Those four weeks in Ethiopia will stay with me.
